Please read /papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/08_open_quantum_dynamics/research-progress/handoffs/10_NATURAL_HAMILTONIAN_BRAINSTORM_CONTINUATION_20261103.md. I want to brainstorm about the form of a natural Hamiltonian, as the note says. First I'd like to draw attention to the formulas for f_i, g_j, their overlap determining the coefficients c, and the multiparticle overlap determining the desired determinant. I think by redefining some of these wavefunctions we might be able to write that as a Hamiltonian expectation value. Can you write down those equations and consider ways that this could be written as an energy expectation value. I am specifically thinking that the theta primitive could be related to the density matrix in equilibrium, possibly using the thermofield double formalism. Please see equation 2.3 from this paper that I published on arxiv in 2020 [https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02713](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.02713) to see the type of equation that I'm talking about. 

Please write any research notes from this discussion within the brainstorm folder within 01_mellin_curvature. I might want to start a new investigation for this, because I think the open quantum dynamics folder is too closely tied to previous ideas, and it might be good to start fresh. Please also save the chat history within 01_mellin_curvature/chat-histories.

I’ll read the handoff and your paper, recover the overlap formulas, and work through possible equilibrium and thermofield-double interpretations. I’ll save any notes in the Mellin-curvature brainstorm folder and the chat history in its chat-histories folder.

The handoff gives exactly the mixed overlaps you have in mind. Equation 2.3 in your paper suggests a useful next step: represent the theta heat trace by a thermofield state, then carry the source’s polynomial energy factor into that state. I’m checking which changes preserve the signed determinant and which produce only its squared magnitude.

I’m using the PDF skill to check the notation in your equation directly. The key distinction so far is that the primitive is a partition function with an \(e^u\) prefactor, while \(\Phi\) includes the energy factor \(P_0(\beta H)=2(\beta H)^2-3\beta H\). Both have exact thermofield representations, but their normalized states differ.

There is a useful redefinition: replace the averaged energy response in \(f_i\) by the corresponding energy-dependent operator acting on a filtered thermofield state. Pairing it with the lifted \(g_j\) preserves every coefficient and determinant exactly, although the \(f_i\) norms change.

I also found a narrow constraint: a single self-adjoint operator cannot map every \(g_i\) to the original \(f_i\) with the same labels, because their cross-overlap matrix is not symmetric. The thermofield construction gives us a way to explore beyond that particular assignment.

The thermofield route now gives an explicit formula for the signed determinant as one expectation value. The observable is a many-copy expression built from the energy responses and moment functions; it is not simply the sum of the particle energies. That leaves a concrete next question: whether one natural interaction or response principle generates these expressions across orders. I’m saving the derivation, including the changed norms and that remaining distinction.

Yes. **Your thermofield suggestion gives an exact way to redistribute the thermal factors between the wavefunctions and an energy observable while preserving the signed determinant.** The remaining question is whether those observables arise from one natural Hamiltonian across all orders.

Start with the original states in \(L^2((0,\infty),du)\):
\[
f_i(u)=\frac{\Phi^{(2i)}(u)}{\sqrt{\Phi(u)}},
\qquad
g_j(u)=m_j(u)\sqrt{\Phi(u)},
\qquad
m_j(u)=\frac{u^{2j}}{(2j)!}.
\]
Writing
\[
c_k=\int_0^\infty m_k(u)\Phi(u)\,du,
\qquad c_k=0\quad(k<0),
\]
complete-source reflection and integration by parts give
\[
\boxed{\langle f_i,g_j\rangle=c_{j-i}.}
\]
Consequently, for finite increasing index lists \(I,J\),
\[
\boxed{
D_{I,J}:=\det[c_{j_b-i_a}]
=
\left\langle
f_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge f_{i_r},
g_{j_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge g_{j_r}
\right\rangle .
}
\]
These are unnormalized states; their normalization involves their respective Gram determinants.

Your equation (2.3) provides the next ingredient. Take
\[
h|n\rangle=E_n|n\rangle,\qquad E_n=\pi n^2,\qquad
Q(\beta)=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\beta E_n}.
\]
This spectrum has a simple geometric realization as a Dirichlet particle on an interval. The corresponding thermofield state is
\[
|\mathrm{TFD}_\beta\rangle
=
\frac1{\sqrt{Q(\beta)}}\sum_{n\ge1}
e^{-\beta E_n/2}|n,\bar n\rangle,
\]
with reduced density matrix
\[
\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta h}}{Q(\beta)}.
\]
Its left-copy expectations reproduce thermal traces, as in equations (2.3)–(2.4) of [your paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2001.02713v1#page=3).

Now set \(\beta=e^{4u}\). The theta primitive is
\[
p(u)=e^uQ(e^{4u}).
\]
Thus, defining
\[
|B(u)\rangle=\sqrt{p(u)}\,|\mathrm{TFD}_{e^{4u}}\rangle,
\]
we have
\[
\boxed{p(u)=\langle B(u)|B(u)\rangle.}
\]
This makes the primitive the normalization of an unnormalized thermofield state.

The source \(\Phi\) also has an immediate energy interpretation:
\[
\Phi(u)=\frac{p''(u)-p(u)}8
=e^u\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[P_0(\beta h)e^{-\beta h}\right],
\qquad P_0(x)=2x^2-3x.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{
\frac{\Phi(u)}{p(u)}
=
\langle \mathrm{TFD}_\beta|
P_0(\beta h_L)
|\mathrm{TFD}_\beta\rangle
=
2\beta^2\langle h^2\rangle_\beta
-3\beta\langle h\rangle_\beta .
}
\]
So the source already measures a combination of the mean energy and its fluctuations.

Because \(\beta E_n\ge\pi\) on our half-line, \(P_0(\beta h)>0\). We can move its square root into the state:
\[
|\Omega(u)\rangle
=
P_0(\beta h_L)^{1/2}|B(u)\rangle
=
e^{u/2}\sum_n
\sqrt{P_0(\beta E_n)}\,e^{-\beta E_n/2}|n,\bar n\rangle.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{\|\Omega(u)\|^2=\Phi(u).}
\]
After normalization, this purifies the **filtered thermal density matrix**
\[
\rho_u^\Phi=
\frac{P_0(\beta h)e^{-\beta h}}
{\operatorname{Tr}[P_0(\beta h)e^{-\beta h}]}.
\]
The temperature-dependent filter matters: this differs from ordinary equilibrium for the original \(h\).

This suggests a particularly useful redefinition of your wavefunctions. Introduce the source-response polynomials
\[
P_{k+1}(x)=4xP_k'(x)+(1-4x)P_k(x),
\qquad R_i(x)=\frac{P_{2i}(x)}{P_0(x)}.
\]
They satisfy
\[
\Phi^{(2i)}(u)
=e^u\sum_n P_{2i}(\beta E_n)e^{-\beta E_n}.
\]
On the enlarged source-coordinate and thermofield space, define
\[
\boxed{
\widetilde f_i(u)=R_i(\beta h_L)\Omega(u),
\qquad
\widetilde g_j(u)=m_j(u)\Omega(u).
}
\]
Now the overlap is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\langle\widetilde f_i,\widetilde g_j\rangle
&=\int_0^\infty
m_j(u)\langle\Omega(u)|R_i(\beta h_L)|\Omega(u)\rangle\,du\\
&=\int_0^\infty m_j(u)\Phi^{(2i)}(u)\,du\\
&=\boxed{c_{j-i}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
**Every unnormalized multiparticle determinant is therefore preserved.** The new \(f_i\) retain the energy-dependent response before thermal averaging. Their norms change by an integrated thermal variance, so normalized overlaps must use the new norms.

We can go one step further and obtain a single expectation value. Since \(\int\Phi=c_0\), the vector-valued wavefunction
\[
\Psi(u)=\frac{\Omega(u)}{\sqrt{c_0}}
\]
is normalized. Let \(U\) denote the source-coordinate operator and \(X=e^{4U}h_L\). Then
\[
\boxed{
c_{j-i}=c_0\langle\Psi|m_j(U)R_i(X)|\Psi\rangle.
}
\]
For \(r\) copies, define the real, self-adjoint multiplication observable
\[
\mathcal E_{I,J}
=
\frac1{r!}
\det_{a,k}[R_{i_a}(X_k)]\,
\det_{b,k}[m_{j_b}(U_k)].
\]
Expanding the determinants gives
\[
\boxed{
D_{I,J}
=
c_0^r
\langle\Psi^{\otimes r}|
\mathcal E_{I,J}
|\Psi^{\otimes r}\rangle .
}
\]
This retains the determinant’s sign. It supplies a concrete many-body energy-observable candidate. The unresolved step is to derive these index-dependent observables from a common interaction or thermal-response principle; the free energy operator \(\sum_k h_k\) does not itself supply that relation.

There is also a useful constraint on the simpler proposal \(Hg_i=f_i\). With the original labels, self-adjointness would require
\[
\langle g_0,Hg_1\rangle=\langle Hg_0,g_1\rangle,
\]
but the two sides would be \(c_{-1}=0\) and \(c_1>0\). Thus that particular assignment cannot work. The thermofield construction above allows distinct preparation operators and avoids imposing it.

My preference is to pursue **the geometric Hamiltonian \(h\), its thermofield state, and the response preparations \(\widetilde f_i,\widetilde g_j\)**. They connect the primitive, equilibrium density, original coefficients, and signed determinant explicitly. The next substantive question is what physical structure could constrain the sign of \(\mathcal E_{I,J}\)’s expectation.

I saved the [derivation and candidate comparison](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/brainstorm/notes/02_THERMOFIELD_SOURCE_STATES_AND_ENERGY_EXPECTATIONS_20261103.md) in the requested brainstorm folder. This chat is registered as **0004** in `01_mellin_curvature/chat-histories`, with capture of this final reply arranged.

Personally, instead of defining a filtered thermal density matrix, I would keep the TFD state and keep the expression as an expectation value of an observable (in that case P_0(\beta h_L)). Also, when you are talking about multiple copies of the system, I think it would probably be more natural to consider multi-particle states. In particular, my guess is that the parameter r in D_{r,k} should be related to the number of particles under consideration. The way you wrote it here, there are r copies of the same system, which doesn't seem as natural.

I’ll recast the formulas using the ordinary TFD state, with \(P_0\) kept in the observable, and make \(r\) the fermion number in an exterior-power sector. The distinction to check is between those fermions and the auxiliary doubling used to purify a thermal state.

The thermofield double also is equivalent to the density matrix formalism for the equilibrium state, I was just pointing out that formula to illustrate how you could get the primitive from these formulas
It is good to keep both pictures in mind

Understood. I’ll keep the density matrix and TFD descriptions side by side as equivalent descriptions of equilibrium; your reference shows how the primitive appears in either. And \(r\) already has an exact particle-number interpretation in the Slater overlap. What remains to establish is how those source-derived particle states relate to the Hamiltonian with energies \(\pi n^2\).

There’s a clean unfiltered choice of orbitals: use \(\sqrt{p(u)}\) as the common envelope and put each thermal response in the preparation of the bra. Their \(r\)-particle Slater overlap still gives \(D_{r,k}\). I’m recording that formulation, with the density matrix and TFD expressions side by side.

Agreed. I put too much emphasis on the purification as a modeling choice. **We should keep the density matrix and TFD as equivalent descriptions of the same equilibrium state**, using whichever makes a particular calculation clearer.

With \(\beta=e^{4u}\), the starting equations are simply
\[
\rho_\beta=\frac{e^{-\beta h}}{Q(\beta)},
\qquad
p(u)=e^uQ(\beta),
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
\Phi(u)
=p(u)\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\rho_\beta P_0(\beta h)\right]
=p(u)\langle\mathrm{TFD}_\beta|
P_0(\beta h_L)|\mathrm{TFD}_\beta\rangle .
}
\]
Here \(P_0(x)=2x^2-3x\) remains an observable. Your example points directly to this relationship between the primitive and equilibrium statistical mechanics.

**Your interpretation of \(r\) as particle number is also exact in the Slater formulation.** There is a useful choice of wavefunctions that respects both preferences. Define
\[
q_i(u)
=\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\rho_\beta P_{2i}(\beta h)\right]
=\frac{\Phi^{(2i)}(u)}{p(u)},
\]
where the \(P_\ell\) are the thermal-response polynomials from the preceding derivation, and set
\[
a_i(u)=\sqrt{p(u)}\,q_i(u),
\qquad
b_j(u)=\frac{u^{2j}}{(2j)!}\sqrt{p(u)}.
\]
The common envelope now comes from the primitive, while the source derivatives enter through equilibrium observables. Their overlap remains
\[
\langle a_i,b_j\rangle
=\int_0^\infty\frac{u^{2j}}{(2j)!}\Phi^{(2i)}(u)\,du
=c_{j-i}.
\]

Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
D_{r,k}
=
\left\langle
a_0\wedge\cdots\wedge a_{r-1},
b_k\wedge\cdots\wedge b_{k+r-1}
\right\rangle .
}
\]
Both states belong to the **\(r\)-fermion sector** of the source-coordinate Hilbert space. The determinant comes from their fermionic exchange symmetry. My previous product-state expectation obscured this interpretation.

For an equilibrium system of \(r\) noninteracting fermions, the corresponding construction would be
\[
H_r=d\Gamma(h)\big|_{\wedge^r\mathcal H},
\qquad
\rho_{\beta,r}=\frac{e^{-\beta H_r}}{Z_r(\beta)},
\]
or equivalently the TFD purification of this entire \(r\)-particle density matrix. Antisymmetry is included in that ensemble; for example,
\[
Z_2(\beta)=\frac12\left[Q(\beta)^2-Q(2\beta)\right].
\]
The auxiliary TFD doubling is separate from the physical particle number \(r\).

The remaining substantive question is how to connect the source-derived Slater states above to the particles governed by the theta-spectrum Hamiltonian \(h\). We already have the particle-number interpretation and the equilibrium source formulas. A natural Hamiltonian explanation should connect those two structures and turn the mixed Slater amplitude into the desired energy or response expectation.

I saved this formulation and your preferences in [Note03](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/brainstorm/notes/03_EQUILIBRIUM_PICTURES_AND_FERMION_NUMBER_20261104.md), and refreshed the chat archive.

I would look at the definitions of a_i and b_j more closely. Specifically, why do you call P_l thermal-response polynomials? I think these definitions should be clearly physically motivated. Also, I tend to like second-quantization formalism, so if you could stick to that notation it will help me understand better. So I would define creation and annihilation operators, and I don't think the wedge products are standard within that formalism.

I’ll examine what operation actually produces the \(P_\ell\), then rewrite the state construction using creation and annihilation operators. I’ll also separate the physical motivation from the algebraic choices made to reproduce the coefficients.

The \(P_\ell\) come from repeated derivatives with respect to \(u=\tfrac14\log\beta\) of an unnormalized thermal trace, including its \(e^u\) prefactor and energy insertion. “Thermal-response polynomials” was my descriptive shorthand, not a standard physical classification.

There is also a modeling choice I should have made explicit: using \(\sqrt{p(u)}\) as a wavefunction treats \(u\) as a state coordinate, although it currently labels inverse temperature. The overlap identities hold, but that physical interpretation still needs justification.

In creation-operator notation, the exact relationship is
\(\{\hat A_i,\hat B_j^\dagger\}=c_{j-i}\); anticommuting the operators through the vacuum then gives the determinant. The \(\hat A_i\) and \(\hat B_j\) are smeared field operators with nonorthogonal profiles, so their same-family anticommutators are Gram matrices, not Kronecker deltas.

The many-particle extension also needs an explicit choice: summing the one-particle observable \(P_0(\beta E_n)\) over occupied modes differs from applying \(P_0\) to the total energy. The latter includes two-particle terms.

Yes—I should have separated the derivation from its physical interpretation. **“Thermal-response polynomials” was my descriptive shorthand, not a standard named family.** Their precise origin is differentiation with respect to logarithmic inverse temperature. And I’ll use creation and annihilation operators throughout.

Start with fermionic energy-mode operators
\[
\{\hat d_n,\hat d_m^\dagger\}=\delta_{nm},
\qquad
\hat H_0=\sum_{n\ge1}E_n\hat d_n^\dagger\hat d_n,
\qquad E_n=\pi n^2.
\]
The partition function appearing in the primitive is the **one-particle sector trace**
\[
Q(\beta)=\operatorname{Tr}_{N=1}e^{-\beta\hat H_0},
\qquad p(u)=e^uQ(e^{4u}).
\]

The physical operation behind the polynomials is familiar:
\[
\partial_\beta e^{-\beta\hat H_0}
=-\hat H_0e^{-\beta\hat H_0}.
\]
Changing inverse temperature inserts energy into a thermal trace. Here there are additional factors because \(\beta=e^{4u}\) and the primitive includes \(e^u\).

For one energy level, write \(x=\beta E\). Direct differentiation gives
\[
\frac{d}{du}\left[e^uP_\ell(x)e^{-x}\right]
=
e^u\left[4xP_\ell'(x)+(1-4x)P_\ell(x)\right]e^{-x}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{P_{\ell+1}(x)=4xP_\ell'(x)+(1-4x)P_\ell(x).}
\]
The terms come from differentiating the insertion, the prefactor, and the Boltzmann weight, respectively.

The initial polynomial
\[
P_0(x)=2x^2-3x
\]
is fixed by the theta-source identity \(\Phi=(p''-p)/8\). Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
\Phi^{(\ell)}(u)
=e^u\operatorname{Tr}_{N=1}
\left[P_\ell(\beta\hat H_0)e^{-\beta\hat H_0}\right].
}
\]
So these are **energy insertions representing logarithmic inverse-temperature derivatives of this particular unnormalized trace**. They are not simply normalized thermal susceptibilities; differentiating a normalized expectation also produces covariance terms.

This explains the polynomials, but only partly motivates the orbitals. Writing
\[
q_i(u)=
\operatorname{Tr}\!\left[\rho_{\beta,1}P_{2i}(\beta\hat H_0)\right],
\]
my definitions were
\[
a_i(u)=\sqrt{p(u)}\,q_i(u),
\qquad
b_j(u)=\frac{u^{2j}}{(2j)!}\sqrt{p(u)}.
\]
Here \(q_i\) has the thermal-derivative interpretation just derived. The \(b_j\) select moment coefficients, as seen from
\[
\cosh(zu)\sqrt{p(u)}
=\sum_{j\ge0}z^{2j}b_j(u).
\]
They therefore describe derivative and moment probes of the source.

**Choosing \(\sqrt p\) as their common wavefunction envelope remains an additional modeling choice.** Equilibrium mechanics gives a family of states indexed by temperature; it does not automatically make \(u\) a particle coordinate or prescribe a coherent wavefunction over temperatures. The overlap identity motivates these profiles mathematically, but I have not yet derived them as natural physical preparations of \(\hat H_0\).

Their exact second-quantized formulation makes that distinction explicit. For the source-coordinate representation, introduce a canonical field
\[
\{\hat\psi(u),\hat\psi^\dagger(v)\}=\delta(u-v),
\qquad
\{\hat\psi(u),\hat\psi(v)\}=0,
\]
and define
\[
\hat A_i^\dagger=\int_0^\infty a_i(u)\hat\psi^\dagger(u)\,du,
\qquad
\hat B_j^\dagger=\int_0^\infty b_j(u)\hat\psi^\dagger(u)\,du.
\]
Their annihilation operators use the conjugate profiles. Then
\[
\boxed{
\{\hat A_i,\hat B_j^\dagger\}
=\langle a_i,b_j\rangle I
=c_{j-i}I.
}
\]
The \(\hat A_i\) and \(\hat B_j\) are smeared creation and annihilation operators. Their same-family anticommutators are their Gram matrices; the profiles are generally nonorthogonal.

Now define the \(r\)-particle states
\[
|A_r\rangle
=\hat A_0^\dagger\cdots\hat A_{r-1}^\dagger|0\rangle,
\qquad
|B_{r,k}\rangle
=\hat B_k^\dagger\cdots\hat B_{k+r-1}^\dagger|0\rangle.
\]
The anticommutation relations give
\[
\boxed{
D_{r,k}
=
\langle0|
\hat A_{r-1}\cdots\hat A_0
\hat B_k^\dagger\cdots\hat B_{k+r-1}^\dagger
|0\rangle
=
\langle A_r|B_{r,k}\rangle .
}
\]
This is the creation-operator version of the earlier expression. The determinant follows from fermionic exchange, and \(r\) counts particles.

There is also a physical choice to resolve when extending the energy observable to several particles. With \(\hat n_n=\hat d_n^\dagger\hat d_n\),
\[
P_0(\beta\hat H_0)
=
\sum_nP_0(\beta E_n)\hat n_n
+
4\beta^2\sum_{n<m}E_nE_m\hat n_n\hat n_m.
\]
Thus applying \(P_0\) to total energy includes two-particle terms, while summing the individual-particle insertions gives a one-body observable. They coincide in the one-particle sector used by the primitive. The determinant construction must tell us which extension is appropriate.

I would therefore keep \(\hat d_n,\hat d_n^\dagger\) as the physical starting point and seek a preparation or observable rule connecting them to \(\hat A_i,\hat B_j\). That connection is the missing physical motivation; naming the profiles does not supply it.

Saved in [Note04](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/brainstorm/notes/04_LOG_TEMPERATURE_INSERTIONS_AND_SECOND_QUANTIZATION_20261104.md).

I think that your definitions of creation operators are a little odd here. Here u is related to the inverse temperature, so it is not a coordinate in your quantum system. The integrals over u should probably be interpreted thermodynamically. So for the moment I would look at fixed u (or \beta). So you have a system that has N particles in a 1-d box with Dirichlet boundary conditions. I would focus on the integrand in the expression for the relevant determinant. What quantity is that related to? 

Another idea I was thinking about is going back to the three dimensional picture and using the integration by parts interpretation of \phi. I'm not sure if the statistical mechanics works out as well though. But it is worth considering.

I’ll keep \(u\) as a thermodynamic parameter and use creation operators for the box’s spatial modes. I’ll work out what the determinant integrand measures at fixed temperature, then check the earlier three-dimensional integration-by-parts formula as an alternative interpretation.

The determinant integrand fixes \(r\) temperature parameters \(u_1,\ldots,u_r\). Setting them all equal makes its columns coincide; the nonzero local quantity at one temperature comes from the limit after dividing out the vanishing temperature differences.

For the box, there is a natural fixed-\(N\) determinant—the \(N\)-particle thermal density kernel. I’m comparing its exchange terms with the target integrand, rather than assuming \(N=r\). The three-dimensional identity also gives a concrete alternative: \(\Phi\) can be expressed through spatial force and curvature terms.
I think some of the 3d work was done in investigations-5/05_radial_theta_collision_geometry

Yes—I found it there, especially Note73 on integration by parts. It gives
\[
\Phi(u)=\tfrac12R^{5/2}\Delta_3A(R),\qquad
A(R)=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi n^2R^2},\quad R=e^{2u}.
\]
I’m using that normalization and retaining the boundary term at \(R=1\).

The three-dimensional construction preserves a useful statistical-mechanical interpretation. \(A(R)=Q(R^2)\) remains the box heat trace, and integration by parts moves the derivatives from \(\Phi\) onto the probe while retaining the endpoint term.

If \(R\) is instead taken as a physical position in a new model, \(A(R)\) is also the local Boltzmann sum for potentials \(V_n(R)=\pi n^2R^2\). In that picture, \(\Delta_3A/A\) is an expectation of force squared minus potential curvature. Adding quantum motion in \(R\) would require checking a new Gibbs kernel.

Yes. **I should remove \(\hat\psi(u)\) from the physical model.** The physical field lives at a position \(x\) in the box; \(u\) labels temperature. The integrals over \(u\) then combine thermodynamic quantities.

I found the three-dimensional construction in `05_radial_theta_collision_geometry`, particularly Notes01 and 73. It gives a useful alternative, with the boundary terms explicitly accounted for.

For the box \(0<x<1\), take
\[
\varphi_n(x)=\sqrt2\sin(n\pi x),\qquad
\hat\psi(x)=\sum_n\varphi_n(x)\hat d_n,
\]
\[
\hat H_0=\sum_n\pi n^2\hat d_n^\dagger\hat d_n,
\qquad
\rho_{\beta,N}=\frac{\Pi_Ne^{-\beta\hat H_0}}{Z_N(\beta)}.
\]
Everything here is at one fixed inverse temperature, with exactly \(N\) particles.

The natural determinant in this system is an **\(N\)-particle thermal density-matrix kernel**. Define the one-particle heat kernel
\[
K_\beta(x,y)=\sum_n e^{-\beta\pi n^2}
\varphi_n(x)\overline{\varphi_n(y)}.
\]
Then
\[
\boxed{
\left\langle
\hat\psi^\dagger(y_1)\cdots\hat\psi^\dagger(y_N)
\hat\psi(x_N)\cdots\hat\psi(x_1)
\right\rangle_{\beta,N}
=
\frac{\det[K_\beta(x_a,y_b)]}{Z_N(\beta)}.
}
\]
On the diagonal, dividing by \(N!\) gives the normalized joint position density. This exact fixed-\(N\) formula is the appropriate starting point for your proposed interpretation. It does not require grand-canonical factorization. [Dean et al., equations (59)–(68)](https://arxiv.org/html/1609.04366v1#S4.SS2)

Now compare that with the actual integrand we have been discussing. Its sign-bearing part is
\[
\Delta_r(\mathbf u)=
\det[\Phi^{(2i)}(u_j)]_{i=0,\ldots,r-1;\,j=1,\ldots,r}.
\]
The remaining factor in the ordered-chamber integral is
\[
\frac{\prod_j u_j^{2k}\prod_{a<b}(u_b^2-u_a^2)}
{\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}(2k+2j)!},
\]
which is positive.

Using the equilibrium formulas, we obtain exactly
\[
\boxed{
\Delta_r(\mathbf u)=
\left(\prod_j p(u_j)\right)
\det\!\left[
\left\langle P_{2i}(\beta_j\hat H_0)\right\rangle_{\beta_j,1}
\right],
\qquad \beta_j=e^{4u_j}.
}
\]
Thus, in this representation, the integrand is a determinant comparing **energy-inserted thermal traces at different temperatures**. Its columns are thermodynamic parameters. Relating it to the physical \(N\)-particle correlation above requires an additional identity.

At a **single common temperature**, the columns coincide, so \(\Delta_r(u,\ldots,u)=0\) for \(r>1\). The meaningful local quantity is its limit after removing the vanishing temperature differences:
\[
\boxed{
\lim_{u_j\to u}
\frac{\Delta_r(\mathbf u)}
{\prod_{a<b}(u_b-u_a)}
=
\frac{p(u)^r}{\prod_{j=0}^{r-1}j!}
\det\!\left[
\left\langle P_{2i+j}(\beta\hat H_0)\right\rangle_{\beta,1}
\right]_{i,j=0}^{r-1}.
}
\]
This is a Wronskian of derivatives of the unnormalized thermal trace, expressed through energy moments at fixed \(\beta\). For \(r=2\), it reduces to
\[
\Phi\Phi'''-\Phi'\Phi''
=
\Phi^2\frac{d}{du}\left(\frac{\Phi''}{\Phi}\right).
\]

I saved the complete derivation in [Note06](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/07_positive_theta_primitives/01_jensen/01_mellin_curvature/brainstorm/notes/06_RADIAL_GREEN_DETERMINANT_DERIVATION_20261104.md). Here is the derivation and its interpretation.

Start with the box energies and theta primitive:
\[
E_n=\pi n^2,\qquad
Q(\beta)=\sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\beta E_n},
\]
\[
R=e^{2u},\qquad \beta=R^2,\qquad
A(R)=Q(R^2),\qquad p(u)=R^{1/2}A(R).
\]
The source is
\[
\Phi(u)=
\sum_{n\ge1}
\left(2E_n^2R^{9/2}-3E_nR^{5/2}\right)e^{-E_nR^2}.
\]

The relevance of three dimensions follows directly from
\[
\Delta_3e^{-aR^2}
=
\left(4a^2R^2-6a\right)e^{-aR^2},
\qquad
\Delta_3=\partial_R^2+\frac2R\partial_R.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\Phi(u)=\frac12R^{5/2}\Delta_3A(R).}
\tag{1}
\]
The coefficient \(6=2\times3\) is precisely what matches the second term of \(\Phi\).

For a probe \(f(u)\), set
\[
F(R)=R^{-1/2}f\!\left(\tfrac12\log R\right).
\]
Differentiating gives
\[
F'(R)=\frac12R^{-3/2}(f'-f),
\qquad
\Delta_3F(R)=\frac14R^{-5/2}(f''-f).
\]
Since \(du=dR/(2R)\), equation (1) yields
\[
\int_0^\infty\Phi f\,du
=
\frac14\int_1^\infty F\,\Delta_3A\,R^2\,dR.
\]
Applying Green’s identity,
\[
\int_1^\infty(F\Delta_3A-A\Delta_3F)R^2dR
=
[R^2(FA'-AF')]_1^\infty.
\]
The theta tail eliminates the outer boundary. The inner boundary remains:
\[
\int_0^\infty\Phi f\,du
=
\frac14\int_1^\infty A\,\Delta_3F\,R^2dR
+\frac14[-A'(1)F(1)+A(1)F'(1)].
\]

Theta reflection,
\[
1+2A(R)=R^{-1}[1+2A(1/R)],
\]
implies
\[
A'(1)=-\frac12A(1)-\frac14.
\]
Substitution gives the scalar identity
\[
\boxed{
\int_0^\infty\Phi(u)f(u)\,du
=
\frac{f(0)}{16}
+\frac{p(0)f'(0)}8
+\frac18\int_0^\infty p(u)\,[f''(u)-f(u)]\,du.
}
\tag{2}
\]
This is the precise transfer from the differentiated source to the undifferentiated primitive.

Now apply it to the coefficient probes
\[
m_j(u)=\frac{u^{2j}}{(2j)!},\qquad
c_j=\int_0^\infty\Phi(u)m_j(u)\,du,
\qquad
d_j=\int_0^\infty p(u)m_j(u)\,du,
\]
with all three quantities set to zero for negative indices. Because
\[
m_j''=m_{j-1},\qquad m_j'(0)=0,\qquad m_j(0)=\delta_{j0},
\]
we obtain
\[
\boxed{
c_j=b\delta_{j0}+\frac{d_{j-1}-d_j}{8},
\qquad b=\frac1{16}.
}
\tag{3}
\]
In particular, \(c_0=b-d_0/8\). This endpoint contribution matters in the determinants.

To carry the calculation all the way to
\[
D_{r,k}=\det[c_{k+j-i}]_{i,j=1}^{r},
\]
it is useful to choose a different, but exactly equivalent, integrand. Define the symmetric polynomial
\[
\mathcal T_{r,k}(\mathbf u)
=
\frac1{r!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_r}
\det[m_{k+j-i}(u_{\sigma(i)})]_{i,j=1}^{r}.
\tag{4}
\]
Expanding the determinant and integrating each row replaces each \(m_j\) by \(c_j\). Symmetrizing does not change the integral. Therefore
\[
\boxed{
D_{r,k}
=
\int_{[0,\infty)^r}
\prod_{i=1}^{r}\Phi(u_i)\,
\mathcal T_{r,k}(\mathbf u)\,d\mathbf u.
}
\tag{5}
\]
There is no additional factorial in this formula: the symmetrization in (4) is an average.

This representation puts the determinant structure into a symmetric multiparticle observable. It also makes the complete Green calculation straightforward.

Write
\[
L_i=\partial_{u_i}^2-1
\]
and define
\[
W_{r,k}^{(q)}(u_1,\ldots,u_q)
=
\left[
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{q}L_i\right)\mathcal T_{r,k}(\mathbf u)
\right]_{u_{q+1}=\cdots=u_r=0}.
\tag{6}
\]
For \(q=0\), this means \(\mathcal T_{r,k}(0,\ldots,0)\).

Apply (2) in every coordinate of (5). All probes remain even in each coordinate, so the first-derivative boundary terms vanish. Each coordinate contributes either its endpoint value, with factor \(b\), or its volume integral, with factor \(1/8\). Symmetry groups the subsets of \(q\) volume coordinates:
\[
\boxed{
D_{r,k}
=
\sum_{q=0}^{r}
\binom rq b^{r-q}8^{-q}
\int_{[0,\infty)^q}
\prod_{i=1}^{q}p(u_i)\,
W_{r,k}^{(q)}(\mathbf u)\,d\mathbf u.
}
\tag{7}
\]

**Equation (7) is the complete determinant-level Green identity.** Its weights contain only the undifferentiated theta primitive. The source derivatives now act on an explicit polynomial observable.

The terms with \(q<r\) are the genuine boundary contributions at \(R_i=1\). Working on the full orthant avoids introducing artificial boundaries where two radii coincide.

There is a useful simplification:
\[
k\ge r
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
W_{r,k}^{(q)}=0\quad(q<r).
\]
Indeed, every index \(k+j-i\) is then positive, so evaluating any row at \(u_i=0\) gives a zero row. Consequently,
\[
\boxed{
D_{r,k}
=
\frac1{8^r}\int_{[0,\infty)^r}
\prod_i p(u_i)\,
W_{r,k}^{(r)}(\mathbf u)\,d\mathbf u,
\qquad k\ge r.
}
\tag{8}
\]

For an explicit check, take \(r=2,k=1\). Then
\[
\mathcal T_{2,1}(u,v)
=
m_1(u)m_1(v)-\frac12[m_2(u)+m_2(v)].
\]
The boundary probe is
\[
W^{(1)}(u)=-\frac12[m_1(u)-m_2(u)],
\]
and the volume probe is
\[
W^{(2)}(u,v)
=
[1-m_1(u)][1-m_1(v)]
+\frac12[m_1(u)-m_2(u)+m_1(v)-m_2(v)].
\]
Equation (7) becomes
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{2,1}
&=-\frac b8(d_1-d_2)
+\frac1{64}\left[(d_0-d_1)^2+d_0(d_1-d_2)\right]\\
&=c_1^2-c_0c_2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]
Dropping the boundary term would lose the first term on the right.

Now consider what these formulas mean thermodynamically.

For the original box, the primitive measure is
\[
p(u)\,du=\frac14\beta^{-3/4}Q(\beta)\,d\beta.
\tag{10}
\]
Thus Green’s identity removes the energy insertions, but the resulting expressions still integrate the box partition function over \(\beta\). Calling \(\sqrt{\beta}\) a radius does not by itself change that fact.

The alternative is to make \(\mathbf R\) an actual spatial coordinate and give a particle with internal label \(n\) the potential
\[
\boxed{V_n(\mathbf R)=E_n|\mathbf R|^2=\pi n^2R^2.}
\tag{11}
\]
At the single bath inverse temperature \(\beta_*=1\), its local internal partition function is
\[
\sum_n e^{-V_n(\mathbf R)}=A(R).
\]
The Hamiltonian’s local level spacing now varies with position; the bath temperature is fixed.

On the exterior region \(\Omega=\{\mathbf R:R\ge1\}\), use the ordinary configurational Gibbs distribution
\[
Z_{\mathrm{conf}}
=
\sum_n\int_\Omega e^{-V_n(\mathbf R)}\,d^3\mathbf R,
\qquad
d\gamma(\mathbf R,n)
=
Z_{\mathrm{conf}}^{-1}e^{-V_n(\mathbf R)}\,d^3\mathbf R.
\tag{12}
\]
Classical kinetic momenta can be included and integrated out.

Keep the radial Jacobian factor in the observable:
\[
J(R)=\frac1{8\pi R^{5/2}}.
\]
Then angular integration gives the exact identity
\[
\boxed{
\int_0^\infty p(u)f(u)\,du
=
Z_{\mathrm{conf}}
\left\langle J(R)f\!\left(\tfrac12\log R\right)\right\rangle_\gamma.
}
\tag{13}
\]
The equilibrium distribution has not been filtered.

The source insertion also acquires a direct spatial meaning. With \(P_0(x)=2x^2-3x\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\nabla V_n|^2-\Delta V_n&=4E_n^2R^2-6E_n,\\
P_0(V_n)&=\frac{R^2}{2}
\left(|\nabla V_n|^2-\Delta V_n\right).
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
It is a force-squared and potential-curvature observable at one temperature.

Let \(\langle\cdot\rangle_{r,1}\) denote the canonical configurational average for \(r\) noninteracting classical particles with these internal levels. For symmetric observables this is the product Gibbs average; the usual \(1/r!\) cancels between numerator and partition function. Equations (5) and (14) give, for every \(r,k\),
\[
\boxed{
D_{r,k}
=
Z_{\mathrm{conf}}^r
\left\langle
\mathcal T_{r,k}\!\left(\tfrac12\log R_1,\ldots,\tfrac12\log R_r\right)
\prod_{i=1}^{r}J(R_i)P_0(V_{n_i}(R_i))
\right\rangle_{r,1}.
}
\tag{15}
\]

This is an exact **fixed-temperature, \(r\)-particle expectation**. Here \(r\) really counts spatial particles in the newly defined model.

Green’s identity rewrites the same expectation as
\[
\boxed{
D_{r,k}
=
\sum_{q=0}^{r}\binom rq b^{r-q}
\left(\frac{Z_{\mathrm{conf}}}{8}\right)^q
\left\langle
\prod_{i=1}^{q}J(R_i)\,
W_{r,k}^{(q)}
\!\left(\tfrac12\log R_1,\ldots,\tfrac12\log R_q\right)
\right\rangle_{q,1}.
}
\tag{16}
\]
When \(k\ge r\), only the \(r\)-particle volume term survives. Otherwise, the lower-dimensional terms account for particles’ coordinates being evaluated at the boundary. They do not require a grand-canonical ensemble: equation (15) already gives the fixed-\(r\) representation.

The density-matrix and TFD pictures remain equivalent for the internal system at each position:
\[
\rho_{\mathrm{int}}(R)=\frac{e^{-R^2h}}{A(R)},
\qquad
|\mathrm{TFD}(R)\rangle
=
\frac1{\sqrt{A(R)}}\sum_n e^{-E_nR^2/2}
|n\rangle_L|n\rangle_{\widetilde L}.
\]
The insertion \(P_0(R^2h)\) stays in the observable in either presentation.

What remains unresolved is the identification with an ordinary energy expectation for quantum particles. The observables in (15)–(16) contain the determinant probe; they are not the total energy \(\sum_iV_{n_i}\), and their sign is not automatic.

For genuine spatial fermions, a natural candidate in your preferred notation would be
\[
\widehat H_3
=
\sum_n\int_\Omega
\widehat\Psi_n^\dagger(\mathbf R)
\left[-\kappa\nabla_{\mathbf R}^2+\pi n^2R^2\right]
\widehat\Psi_n(\mathbf R)\,d^3\mathbf R,
\]
with canonical anticommutation relations and a specified boundary condition. But its equilibrium spatial density involves the quantum heat kernel, rather than simply \(e^{-V_n}\); fermionic exchange also changes the multiparticle distribution. Matching those quantities to the determinant is the next substantive step. Purifying that state into a TFD leaves the same matching problem.
